analysis.one_liner: Lets bankruptcy judges cut what struggling homeowners owe on their mortgages so they can keep their homes.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced in January 2009 and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let a homeowner in Chapter 13 bankruptcy, facing a foreclosure notice, ask a judge to rewrite their mortgage: cutting the loan balance down to what the house is actually worth, setting a fixed interest rate at the standard market mortgage yield plus a risk premium, stretching repayment up to 40 years, and wiping out prepayment penalties. Today, bankruptcy law treats a primary-residence mortgage differently from almost every other secured debt — it cannot be reduced to the home's value even when the home is worth far less than the loan. The bill would also have waived the pre-bankruptcy credit counseling requirement for people with a foreclosure notice, blocked claims tainted by violations of consumer protection laws even after a foreclosure judgment, and barred lenders from collecting fees they did not properly notice and document during the case.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners who are underwater on their mortgage and facing foreclosure would gain a way to keep their homes: a judge could write the loan down to the home's current value and set terms they can actually pay, instead of letting the lender foreclose on a house worth less than the debt.

how_it_helps.text: A Chapter 13 debtor who has received a foreclosure notice could have the mortgage reduced to the current value of the home, with adjustable-rate adjustments prohibited, reduced, or delayed.
The rewritten loan would be repaid over up to 40 years at a fixed rate equal to the most recently published conventional mortgage yield set by the Federal Reserve, plus a reasonable premium for risk.

Prepayment penalties on a primary-residence mortgage could be waived in the bankruptcy plan, and lenders could not collect fees, costs, or charges incurred during the case unless they noticed them in time and proved they were lawful, reasonable, and covered by the security agreement.
A homeowner with a foreclosure notice would not have to complete the credit counseling requirement before filing Chapter 13.

A court would have to disallow a mortgage claim subject to remedies for violations of the Truth in Lending Act or other consumer protection laws, even after a foreclosure judgment had already been entered.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and investors holding home loans would bear the cost: when a home is worth less than the loan, they would be paid only the home's value, at a market-rate interest with a risk premium rather than whatever the original contract charged, and they would lose prepayment penalties and undocumented fees.

drawbacks.text: When the home is worth less than the loan, the lender's claim is cut to the home's value, so lenders would recover less than the full balance on rewritten mortgages [S3]. Critics of this approach have long argued that the risk would be passed to all future borrowers through higher mortgage rates — an argument the bill itself engages by explicitly authorizing a risk premium on top of the Federal Reserve market yield [S3].

The relief is narrow: it applies only to debtors who have received a foreclosure notice, the lender keeps its lien until the reduced claim is paid or the debtor's discharge, and the judge must find the modification is in good faith — so it would not reach every underwater homeowner, only those already in foreclosure [S3].
The bill would apply immediately to bankruptcy cases already pending at enactment, changing the rules on loans made years earlier [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a family about to lose a home worth less than what they owe, the benefit is direct and large: a monthly payment they can afford instead of a foreclosure. The cost falls on mortgage lenders, who argue it would raise borrowing costs for everyone; the bill limits that exposure by paying lenders at market rate plus a risk premium and requiring a judicial good-faith finding. On balance this is a targeted trade — homeowners and lenders splitting the loss on an already-failed loan, rather than the lender foreclosing and the homeowner losing everything.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the Helping Families Save Their Homes in Bankruptcy Act on January 6, 2009, at the depth of the foreclosure crisis.
Ten Democratic senators cosponsored the bill.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary on January 6, 2009.
The action record shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever followed; the bill died in committee when the 111th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and investors holding home mortgages came out ahead: their loans remained unmodifiable in bankruptcy, so the loss on underwater loans stayed with the homeowner in foreclosure, and no judge could ever write a principal balance down under this law.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 6, 2009, and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Patrick Leahy
against.what_they_did: The Judiciary Committee, which he chaired, never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill in the two years after it was referred.

against.name: Mortgage and banking industry
against.what_they_did: Fought the bankruptcy mortgage-modification proposal throughout the 111th Congress, warning it would raise mortgage rates; the bill never advanced to any vote.

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: His 2009 housing plan publicly endorsed letting bankruptcy judges modify mortgages, but the administration did not press Senate leaders to bring the bill to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no party split appears in the record; all ten cosponsors were Democrats, and the Democratic-controlled Judiciary Committee took no action, while opposition was voiced by the mortgage industry rather than any on-record party bloc.

industries.note: The bill cuts their claims to the home's current value, caps interest at a market yield plus a risk premium, and bars them from collecting prepayment penalties and undocumented fees. Their interest in blocking it ran against underwater homeowners facing foreclosure.

industries.industry: Investors holding home-mortgage debt and mortgage-backed securities
industries.note: When a home's value is below the loan balance, the claim is reduced to the home's value, so these investors would recover less than the full principal on modified loans. Their gain from the bill's death was that foreclosure losses stayed with the borrower.
